why: The final array is fixed once you pick its first height b: b, b+1, b+2, ... or b, b-1, .... Heights can only go up, so b must lift every target above its original, and since the cost grows with b, the greedy choice is the smallest feasible b.
hints: Once you choose the first height of the final array, is the rest of it determined?

Ascending target i is b + i, which needs b ≥ structures[i] - i for every i. Each extra unit of b costs n more, so take the minimum b = max(structures[i] - i). For descending, the target is b - i, so b = max(structures[i] + i).
Compute both bases in one pass, sum (target - original) for each pattern, and return the smaller sum. O(n) time, O(1) space.
pitfalls: You can only increase, so the base is forced up by the tightest position, not chosen by a median.
Totals can exceed 32 bits on large inputs.
constraints:
• 1 <= structures.length <= 10^5 (not stated in the source)
  • 0 <= structures[i] <= 10^9 (not stated in the source)
  • The answer can exceed 32 bits; use a 64-bit integer.
